tagline.text: The Paris of Negros, lined with the wooden mansions of sugar barons

children.text: A small city north of Bacolod, where more than 30 old mansions built during the sugar boom are designated national cultural treasures, earning it the nickname "the Paris of Negros." You can walk through mansion museums, a silver-domed cathedral, and a century-old bakery all in a single day.
Silay is a city in Negros Occidental province, in the northwest of Negros Island, about
14km

north of the provincial capital, Bacolod. Bacolod-Silay International Airport sits within the city, making it the first gateway for a Negros trip, but many travelers only pass through the airport and miss the old town itself. The city's name comes from the kansilay tree that once grew in the area, and it carries the legend of Princess Kansilay, who defended the village against pirates.
Starting in the
mid-19th century

, as the Negros plains were converted into sugarcane plantations, Silay became a city of hacendero families who grew wealthy from the sugar trade. They decorated their mansions with furniture and chandeliers imported from Europe and sent their children to study there, and with a constant stream of concerts, plays, and balls, Silay earned the nicknames "the Paris of Negros" and "the cultural and intellectual center of Negros." More than 30 mansions built during that era still stand today, designated as cultural treasures by the National Historical Commission.
Silay is also significant in Philippine revolutionary history. On
November 5, 1898

, Silay residents gathered at the corner of what is now Cinco de Noviembre Street and marched on the Spanish garrison, which surrendered without a drop of blood shed after negotiations. A street name and a monument commemorating this day stand in the middle of the old town.

The old town clusters within about a 1km radius around the cathedral and plaza, making it easy to explore on foot. It suits travelers who love old mansions, museums, church architecture, and old-fashioned breads and sweets, and it also works well as a half-day to full-day trip from Bacolod, or a stop on the way to the airport.
A living history museum restored from the mansion of Victor Gaston, begun in
. You can see the spacious living room, bedrooms, kitchen, and period furniture of a French-descended sugar planter family exactly as they were, making it the top first stop on a Silay trip.

blocks.title: The art collection of Hofileña Ancestral House

children.text: The Hofileña family mansion on Cinco de Noviembre Street holds works by Filipino masters such as Juan Luna, Félix Resurrección Hidalgo, and Fernando Amorsolo, along with a drawing from Rizal's student days. A family member often gives the tour personally, so there's plenty to hear.
A mansion nicknamed the "Pink House" for its pink exterior walls, displaying everyday items of a sugar baron family — old dolls, textbooks, and kitchen tools.
A church designed by Italian architect Lucio Bernasconi and completed in
; its silver dome, about
tall, is a rare sight in Negros Occidental. The plaza in front of the church is a popular spot for an evening walk.
Silay's oldest bakery, opened in the

, known for its "guapple pie," a fruit pie combining guava and apple, and lumpia ubod, spring rolls filled with heart of palm. It occupies the ground floor of an old mansion, giving it a fine atmosphere too.

blocks.title: A walk along Rizal Street's heritage buildings

children.text: Rizal Street is lined with old commercial buildings with shops on the ground floor and living quarters above. Look out for the twin mansions and the 1898 revolution monument too.
The coastal village of Balaring, about
10–15 minutes
from downtown by car, has a cluster of seafood restaurants built over the water, perfect for dinner while watching the sunset over the Guimaras Strait.

blocks.title: A day trip to the Patag plateau

children.text: Patag, a plateau village inside Northern Negros Natural Park, was the Japanese army's last stronghold during World War II and has a cool climate, waterfalls, and war relics. The mountain road is rough, so a 4x4 vehicle or a local tour is needed.

The road to Patag can become difficult for vehicles when it rains, so during the wet season, ask the local tourism office or your lodging about road conditions first.
From Manila to Bacolod-Silay Airport (BCD) takes about
1 hour 10 minutes
, with daily flights from Philippine Airlines, Cebu Pacific, and others. There are also direct flights from Cebu, Davao, and elsewhere.
The airport is within Silay City, about
15–20 minutes
from the old town by taxi or Grab, for around
. You can also take a tricycle or transfer to a jeepney from outside the airport, but a taxi is more convenient if you have luggage.
From downtown Bacolod, head to the North Bus Terminal, then take a jeepney or Ceres bus bound for Silay or Victorias. It takes about
30–45 minutes
, for around
Get off near the plaza in front of the cathedral, and the main mansions are all within about
10 minutes
on foot. Just tell the driver to drop you at "Plaza" or "City Hall."
About
25–40 minutes
from downtown Bacolod by taxi or Grab, for around
. If traveling in a group, a half-day chartered vehicle (about
) combining Silay with The Ruins in Talisay is also a good option.
From Iloilo, a fast craft to Bacolod takes about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
, and from Bacolod port it's about
30–40 minutes
to Silay by taxi.
Walking is best in the old town. Use a tricycle for Balaring coast or the airport (about
for a short ride, about
chartered), and it helps to agree on a waiting fee with the driver in advance for your return.
Western Negros has its dry season from
December to May
, the best time for a heritage walk.
December–February
is relatively cool, while
March–May
sees midday temperatures climb to
, so schedule museum visits for midday and street walks for morning and late afternoon.
June–November

is the wet season with frequent afternoon showers, but since this is a city trip, it causes little disruption. The mountain road to the Patag plateau does become dangerous in heavy rain, though. Festivals include the Kansilay Festival around
June 12
, marking the city's founding anniversary, and the Cinco de Noviembre commemoration on
November 5
. In October, lodging around the airport gets crowded because of neighboring Bacolod's MassKara Festival.

Silay town has a few small hotels, pensions, and guesthouses converted from old mansions, at about

a night. Options are limited, so most travelers stay around Lacson Street in Bacolod and visit Silay as a day trip. If you need to catch an early flight, staying in Silay near the airport is convenient.

Silay is known for a snack culture rooted in the kitchens of sugar baron families. The most iconic dish is lumpia ubod, heart of palm wrapped in a thin crepe and served with a sweet garlic sauce, and El Ideal's guapple pie, baye-baye (coconut simmered with sugar), thin rolled wafer cookies called barquillos, and milk candy pastillas also make good gifts. For lunch, try chicken inasal or Filipino home cooking at a downtown restaurant, and for dinner, order shrimp, crab, oysters, and grilled fish by weight along the Balaring coast.
The mansion museums generally open Tuesday to Sunday,
, and close on Mondays and some holidays. Avoid visiting on a Monday.
The tourism office near city hall can give you a map marking the heritage houses. Knowing which mansions are open to the public and which are private homes makes planning your route easier.
Most of the designated heritage mansions are still private homes where families live. View them only from outside, and don't enter without permission even if a door is open.
At Balay Negrense, you may need to remove your shoes or wear slip covers indoors, so easy-to-remove footwear is a good idea.
El Ideal's popular pies and lumpia sometimes sell out by afternoon, so it's best to go in the morning or for an early lunch.
Since it's close to the airport, you can also leave your luggage before departing from Bacolod and spend a half-day exploring. Arrange your taxi to the airport in advance.
The Ruins in Talisay, near Bacolod, is in the same direction as Silay, so they pair well in a single day. Schedule Silay in the morning and The Ruins at dusk.
Admission fees and jeepney fares are often cash-only, so carry plenty of small change.
Don't touch the antique furniture, ceramics, or paintings inside the museums, and follow any no-photography or no-flash signs.
Sidewalks in the old town are often narrow and uneven. When walking on the road, watch out for tricycles and motorbikes.
Operating hours and admission fees change often due to family circumstances or restoration work. Check with the tourism office or the museum's notices before visiting.
The mountain road to the Patag plateau is steep and slippery when it rains. Use an experienced driver and a 4x4 vehicle, and don't push it during the wet season.
Balaring seafood restaurants price by weight, so confirm the price per kilogram and the cooking fee before ordering.
